thread.title: LDL And Natural Gas Statistics: You Can't Handle The Truth!

author: Steve Frechette
title: LDL And Natural Gas Statistics: You Can't Handle The Truth!
text:
In my first natural gas article last December, I wrote:
The fundamental forces of gas production are undeniably leaning bearish... Does that mean gas can't rally? HELL NO. The most important force in the natural gas market is Mother Nature. Extremely cold weather is needed to offset bearish production levels and reinforce damaged Bull psyches.
When it comes to my favorite commodity, the weather is ALWAYS the most important factor especially during the amped-up winter trading period. Nine months of bullish weather from early March 2018 through early December turbocharged the bulls and caught many large hedge funds offside culminating in the November price spike and massive short squeeze. Bearish production fundamentals were masked by the unrelenting demand for AC during a hot Summer, a historic cold April with withdrawals stretching near May, and the fatal blow, a triple-digit withdrawal before Thanksgiving capping off a cold fall. Big price volatility always attracts a lot of attention and many commentators made bold claims about new demand leading to sustainable price gains. Some argued you could kiss "lower for longer" gas prices goodbye permanently. I've been a natural gas follower for a long time and these claims didn't add up, but maybe I was wrong. The best trait you can have as a commodities investor is the ability to stand back and consider the other side of the argument assuming your original opinion is dead wrong. It's a great exercise to make sure you've considered all possibilities.
What evidence do we have to prove the recent price spike was primarily due to a long stretch of bullish weather? I'm imagining the famous scene from a Few Good Men with Jack Nicholson squaring off against Tom Cruise.
The Bulls can't handle the truth!
Exhibit A: The Price Curve Trading is a strange game. Sometimes you feel like you're in the twilight zone watching the price curve do crazy things based on transitory factors. The funny thing about the recent spike was the curve didn't do anything crazy at all. The curve behaved extraordinarily rational confining the gains to the near-term winter months with the non-winter months barely moving higher. At the height of the panic, the non-winter 2019 contracts were stuck at an unimpressive strip of ~$2.88 confounding many analysts.
Shut the front door! Spot and front month prices spiked to near $5 on the mid-November arctic blast and the April contract barely reached $3? Surely a structural change in supply and demand would've moved the non-winter months to at least $3.50+ to stimulate higher production throughout 2019?
The price curve isn't perfect, but it does reflect the best guess of a large group of interested parties who have skin in the game every time they put capital at risk. The curve has been telling us for years natural gas faces an uphill climb based on all available information today. Periods of anomalous weather or black swan events like a major pipeline explosion can drive short-term fluctuations, but it's hard to outrun average temperatures over the long term.
Here's a snapshot of today's CME price curve :
Bottom Line: The spread between the winter and the non-winter contracts clearly shows a market that is not concerned with long-term supply.
Exhibit B: Weather Panic For nine months, we experienced bullish weather starting with a historic cold April and finishing with a chilly fall. The seemingly never-ending bullish revisions led to extreme bullish market sentiment and abnormally low EIA storage. Weather ALWAYS reverts to average temperatures, but most of the natural gas trading profits come during these periods of irrational weather exuberance. It usually doesn't take nine+ months for temps to revert, but when it does, you can bet on extreme market volatility and that's exactly what we've experienced since the October breakout.
At the end of November, there was near universal consensus December would be colder than average and most likely colder than 2017. Forecasting weather must be the toughest job on the planet because no one gets it consistently right, and forecasting beyond the next two weeks seems like a pointless exercise. After a cold start, forecasters dialed back end of the month expectations in response to weather models trending towards a warm finish. Front month prices rapidly corrected from the $4.50 to $4.70 range down to $3.60 to $3.80.
Why the sudden move? Weather panic works in both directions. The coldest period last winter was from December 10th through January 22nd. Last week the bulls were suddenly confronted with the prospect of bearish weather for the first time in a long time combined with difficult year over year storage comparisons. The rush for the exits was on and prices quickly broke through technical support levels.
The table below shows the year ago withdrawals compared to the five-year averages. This data is available for free on the EIA Natural Gas website .
Week Ending Last Year's Withdrawal (BCF) Five-Year Average (BCF) 12/15/17 -182 -152 12/22/17 -112 -122 12/29/17 -206 -117 01/05/18 -359 -209 01/12/18 -183 -178 01/19/18 -288 -167 01/26/18 -99 -162 Total -1,429 -1,107 Withdrawals last year were 29% greater than the five-year average due to historic cold weather. This was always going to be a challenging period for the bulls. In the absence of equivalent cold weather, the y-o-y EIA deficit will contract substantially over the coming weeks. Furthermore, December is a key period for winter weather intensity. The risk premium for February and March goes down when you lose potential consumption in December.
Bottom Line: The price action over the past nine weeks screams weather-induced panic in both directions. If the market sensed a structural change to the supply/demand balance, prices would be more resilient to forecast changes, and the gains would be distributed across the 2019 curve.
Exhibit C: Natural Gas E&Ps This is a tough section for me because I've rooted for the gas E&Ps for a long time given their critical importance to the U.S. economy and the independence gas provides from foreign energy sources. Unfortunately, you can't hide from the fact Wall Street hates the gas sector. We can debate this for the next year, but it comes down to one simple fact. Hydraulic fracturing brought a technology revolution to the gas industry starting in 2007. Increased efficiency and lower production costs have enabled record North American output with a big assist from associated gas from oil drilling.
With Henry Hub prices rallying to $5+ in mid-November and elevated prices holding into mid-December, the casual observer would likely expect a cash bonanza to follow for the gas E&Ps. Stock prices must have soared in response to the big price jump, right? The results couldn't be more opposite. The majority of gas E&Ps hedge large volumes six to fourteen months ahead to reduce weather risk and guarantee cash flow to creditors. Hedging mutes the impact of near-term price changes and transfers the gains to the futures holders and storage owners. Additionally, many gas E&Ps diversified production assets into NGLs and oil. Not very helpful with WTI cratering over the past ten weeks.
Gulfport ( GPOR ) is near $8, Chesapeake ( CHK ) near $2.15, Range ( RRC ) near $11, Antero ( AR ) under $11, Southwestern Energy ( SWN ) near $3.70, EQT ( EQT ) under $19, CNX ( CNX ) under $12, and Apache ( APA ) near $29. Cabot ( COG ) is arguably the best operator with the lowest production costs and smallest hedge book in the industry, and not even Cabot can escape the negative sentiment. The charts are simply untouchable.
For anyone thinking I'm cherry-picking data, I encourage you to look at the two-, three-, or five-year charts for these companies. The bloodbath has gone on for a long time. A picture is worth a thousand words. I'll let the charts speak for the sector.
Bottom Line: Wall Street crushed the gas sector with almost every stock trading at multi-year lows despite the powerful rally in the front month contracts. This says a lot about where Wall Street sees the gas curve going in 2019 and the sustainability of higher prices.
I rest my case. The evidence presented strongly suggests "lower for longer" gas prices are here to stay. They never left if you've been paying attention to the full price curve.
Positioning for the Remainder of Winter Is natural gas doomed forever? Absolutely not. The last major bottom came in the spring of 2016 when crashing oil prices synchronized with a warm winter leading to a rare period of lower North American gas production. Weak natural gas prices persisted from Q4-2015 into Q1-2016 bottoming near $1.60. The market was clearly signaling 'STOP immediately' to the gas E&Ps and the message was received. The Baker Hughes gas rig count bottomed at 82 in the spring of 2016. This was a jaw-dropping number for long-term industry followers. DUC inventories were harvested and capex budgets were slashed. At the same time, WTI crashed below $30 in response to the 'OPEC Flood' policy and this led to lower associated gas production. This perfect storm of forces combined to reduce North American gas production in early 2017 and delivered a solid base for the next expansion cycle that we're still in today.
That was a nice walk down memory lane, but how do we make money for the remainder of this winter? The market is hypersensitive right now because you have strong bearish production fundamentals battling bullish demand. After nine months of bullish weather, market sentiment was clearly offsides to the bullish extreme setting up a swift correction last week when weather disappointment finally arrived.
Weather will continue driving near-term prices. It's possible we could have a strong Polar Vortex for the entire month of January, or maybe we'll get a super warm finish for the remainder of winter. Prices go to the moon for the first case and crash below $2 for the second. No one knows with high confidence what Mother Nature will deliver for the remainder of winter, and they're lying to you if they claim otherwise. The reality is we have to plan for average weather and look for opportunities when market sentiment gets out of line. For aggressive investors, money can be made from both sides by monitoring technical levels and watching daily weather updates. For investors with less time to track HDD changes in the Euro and GFS, AVOID TRADING THE COMMODITY!! The past two months are all the proof you need crazy things really do happen in the winter natural gas market. If you're bullish natural gas and don't have much spare time, buy Cabot or National Fuel Gas ( NFG ) and check back in a few quarters.
It's likely there are still many trapped bulls at $4+ and that means a lot of overhead resistance for rallies. If we can get to Jan 4th with ~2,500 BCF in EIA storage, there will be a lot of pressure on the bulls given the short window to get to March 24th (1/4/19 to 3/24/19 = 80 days). The 2019 price curve faces a lot of pressure from bullish 2018 weather. Year over year storage comparisons get difficult in early March and stay that way through early December 2019. The price curve appears to know this already and maybe that's why the non-winter months can't get above $3.
Thank you for reading and good luck with your trades.
